Israel likely to lose Gaza genocide case if ICJ follows Myanmar ruling, Tel Aviv scholar says
Israel will probably lose the genocide case brought by South Africa if the International Court of Justice (ICJ) applies the reasoning it used last week to find Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya, an Israeli international law scholar has said.
“It is very bad that we have reached this point. It is a real earthquake,” said Eliav Lieblich, a professor at Tel Aviv University’s law faculty.
“Before jumping to conspiracy theories about the court, Israel has mainly itself to blame,” he wrote in a series of posts in Hebrew on X. “Even if you disagree with the majority on every legal point, no reasonable country should come anywhere close to falling short of the standards it set. In many respects, Netanyahu’s government dug this hole itself.”
The ICJ on Thursday concluded in a 9-6 decision that Myanmar's security forces had committed genocide against the Rohingya population in northern Rakhine State during the military's 2017 operations.
The judgment, the first time the UN's highest court has found a state responsible for genocide, offers South Africa a significant legal precedent in its case accusing Israel of committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, particularly over how judges assess genocidal intent when a state claims its military actions are driven by security objectives.

The number of active Rafale fighter jets in the Indian Air Force has fallen to 32 from 35 in the latest edition of an international military aviation directory, which has stirred renewed scrutiny of India's May 2025 military confrontation with Pakistan.
The revised figures, which appear in the 2027 World Air Forces directory published by British aviation magazine FlightGlobal, have renewed questions about the extent of Indian losses during Operation Sindoor.
Following the 22 April 2025 Pahalgam attack in Indian-administered Kashmir, India launched the military campaign on 7 May and attacked several targets deep inside Pakistan.
In the largest jet engagements of the 21st century, over 114 fighter jets were mobilised and engaged across the border.
Some 72 Indian Air Force (IAF) aircraft and 42 Pakistan Air Force (PAF) aircraft engaged each other in a confrontation that lasted roughly 50 minutes, according to military briefings and defence analyses.
Pakistan claimed to have shot down six Indian military aircraft, including three Rafales, during the confrontation.
New Delhi disputed the scale of Islamabad's claims but did not publish a detailed account of its own aircraft losses.
During a military briefing on 11 May, Air Marshal Awadhesh Kumar Bharti acknowledged that India had suffered aircraft losses but declined to identify the number or types involved.
“We are in a combat scenario and losses are a part of combat,” Bharti said.

Israel will probably lose the genocide case brought by South Africa if the International Court of Justice (ICJ) applies the reasoning it used last week to find Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya, an Israeli international law scholar has said.
“It is very bad that we have reached this point. It is a real earthquake,” said Eliav Lieblich, a professor at Tel Aviv University’s law faculty.
“Before jumping to conspiracy theories about the court, Israel has mainly itself to blame,” he wrote in a series of posts in Hebrew on X. “Even if you disagree with the majority on every legal point, no reasonable country should come anywhere close to falling short of the standards it set. In many respects, Netanyahu’s government dug this hole itself.”
The ICJ on Thursday concluded in a 9-6 decision that Myanmar's security forces had committed genocide against the Rohingya population in northern Rakhine State during the military's 2017 operations.
The judgment, the first time the UN's highest court has found a state responsible for genocide, offers South Africa a significant legal precedent in its case accusing Israel of committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, particularly over how judges assess genocidal intent when a state claims its military actions are driven by security objectives.
To prove the genocide, the ICJ first had to prove that genocidal acts were committed, then that there was a “specific intent” by the Myanmar state to destroy the group.

The proposal advocated for dialogue with the US over curbing the ICC's ability to pursue cases involving nationals of countries that aren't members of the court, such as the US, Israel and Russia.
MEE understands that Washington's G7 allies, including the UK, Germany and Italy, expressed a readiness to discuss the proposal with the US but were reluctant to advocate the idea publicly.

It’s in keeping with his family history. Mulipola’s great-grandfather, Mataʻutia Karauna Solomona, was a Samoan resistance leader and secretary of the Mau movement, which sought to free Western Samoa of colonial rule in the 1920s and 1930s.
Solomona’s arrest resulted in a massacre of unarmed protesters by the New Zealand military and police.

Samoans around the world grew more curious, and have carried the flag at Palestine demonstrations. But the response was not all positive.
“Christian Zionism has got quite a strong stranglehold on Samoans and other people of the Pacific,” Mulipola tells Middle East Eye in a video call interview.

Dr Amina Shareef, a researcher of anti-Muslim racism, says that the destruction unfolding in Gaza, Iran and Lebanon is part of a longer history of anti-Muslim racism that has made mass Muslim suffering and death politically permissible.
She says that Islamophobia is not simply a matter of prejudice or discrimination, but a global system of racial power that constructs Muslims and those identified as Muslim as security threats, allowing violence against them to be justified in the name of security.
Central to this system is the figure of the Muslim terrorist, which portrays Muslim political agency as inherently threatening. Shareef says that this logic extends beyond surveillance, detention and militarised borders to warfare, political abandonment and the destruction of the conditions necessary for life.
She identifies Palestine as a key site where contemporary security practices and technologies of control have been refined and reproduced elsewhere, a process she describes through the concept of the “Palestine boomerang”. Although conflicts in Iran, Lebanon, Kashmir, Syria, Yemen, Iraq and Afghanistan have distinct histories, she argues that they reveal a recurring pattern in which Muslim populations are portrayed as threats and their suffering becomes easier to justify.
Shareef concludes that confronting anti-Muslim racism is ultimately a struggle to protect life and human dignity. She calls for sustained resistance to systems that expose entire populations to premature death, arguing that the responsibility to seek justice remains even when the outcome is uncertain.

Trump claims he predicted drops in oil prices, stock market and hits from Iran after Democratic win in midterm elections
US president Donald Trump claimed that he predicted a stock market decline as well as harsher attacks from Iran after the Democratic victory in the recent midterm elections.
"As everyone remembers, I predicted two things concerning the November 3rd Midterm Elections. One, that if the Democrats win, the Stock Markets would go down, substantially, which they have, and two, that the Islamic Republic of Iran... will grow more aggressive in their attacks, which has also occurred," he wrote in a post on his platform Truth Social.
Trump added that Iran "launched more drones and missiles in the last week than at any time for over a year," but claimed that the attacks have "all been knocked down, and done no damage".
"Iranian leaders consider the Democrats weak, ineffective, and Country destroying, but I won’t let that happen! Both the Dems and Iran fought like hell to keep the Oil price up as long as possible and, since the Election, the Oil price has dropped by a record level," the American president further claimed.
Trump went onto describe the elections as "very strange".
In another post, he questioned the drop in oil prices, saying: "Isn’t it interesting that Oil prices have dropped precipitously after the Midterm Elections? I said that was going to happen. The whole thing is a Giant Hoax!"

Eisenkot condemns 'Jewish terrorism' near Ramallah as US congressman calls for accountability
Israeli politician Gadi Eisenkot has condemned a series of arson attacks by settlers in the occupied West Bank as "Jewish terrorism", accusing far-right ministers Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben Gvir of fuelling violence against Palestinians.
Overnight into Sunday, Israeli settlers attacked three Palestinian villages near Ramallah, setting fire to vehicles and spray-painting racist slogans on residential buildings.
Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, described the attacks as "Jewish terrorism in every sense of the word" and called on the government and security establishment to take tougher action against violent settlers.
"The acts of sabotage carried out by extremist groups setting fire to vehicles and homes undermine regional stability, endanger lives and seriously harm Israel's national security and foreign relations," he wrote on X.
Opposition leader Yair Lapid also condemned the attacks, calling them "Jewish terrorism" caused by government negligence.
"Jewish terrorism is the product of criminal negligence on the part of the Israeli government," Lapid said. "By remaining silent, government ministers are deliberately encouraging these pogroms."
"When we form a government, we will tackle this terrorism and restore governance, law and order," he added.
In the United States, Democratic Congressman Josh Gottheimer condemned the attacks and called for accountability.
"These incidents warrant a full and thorough investigation," Gottheimer wrote on X, adding that vigilante justice had "no place" in society.
Israeli police said they had opened investigations into arson, vandalism and property damage.

Netanyahu, Eisenkot parties end talks without deal on forming government
The parties of caretaker Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his rival Gadi Eisenkot concluded a new round of talks on Sunday without reaching an agreement on a possible coalition government, which would require concessions from both sides.
Delegations from Eisenkot’s Yashar party and Netanyahu’s Likud met for four hours at a hotel in Herzliya, near Tel Aviv, following a first round of discussions last Sunday.
“The latest round of coalition talks… has concluded. The two sides outlined their positions on a range of substantive issues and discussed them in detail,” the two parties said in a joint statement.
“A follow-up meeting will be held,” they added, without specifying a date or revealing any other details.
A former army chief of staff, Eisenkot has until 6 December to form a government, with the possibility of a 14‑day extension, after October elections failed to give either camp an absolute majority.
His 48-member bloc, which needs 61 lawmakers to reach a majority, remains divided over whether to build a coalition through an alliance with ultra‑Orthodox parties, a rapprochement with Arab parties, or a national unity government with Likud.
Netanyahu is pushing for a national unity government, which could see a rotation of the premiership between the two men.

Cop31 ends in failure as countries reject climate deal over fossil fuels
The United Nations climate summit in Turkey became the longest-ever UN climate conference on Sunday as negotiations over a final agreement descended into deadlock, with the European Union and several other countries formally rejecting the proposed text.
The talks in Antalya, known as Cop31, continued more than 44 hours beyond their scheduled Friday conclusion, surpassing the previous record set by Cop25 in Madrid in 2019.
The latest draft, presented by the Turkish and Australian presidencies in an attempt to bridge divisions between countries, failed to secure consensus over its omission of explicit references to fossil fuels and disagreements over climate finance.
At the closing plenary, Cop31 President Murat Kurum acknowledged that countries had failed to agree on the proposed document.
“We have done our utmost. Ultimately, we have not imposed this text on anyone, nor have we issued an ultimatum such as a ‘take it or leave it’ demand,” Kurum said.
This is a developing story. We'll bring more updates shortly.

Israeli politician Gadi Eisenkot has condemned a series of arson attacks by settlers in the occupied West Bank as "Jewish terrorism", accusing far-right ministers Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben Gvir of fuelling violence against Palestinians.
Settlers attacked the villages of Deir al-Sudan, Deir Abu Mashal and Kafr Malik, near Ramallah, overnight between Saturday and Sunday, setting fire to Palestinian-owned vehicles and spraying racist graffiti on homes, according to Palestinian media reports.
Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, described the attacks as "Jewish terrorism in every sense of the word" and called on the government and security establishment to take tougher action against violent settlers.
"The acts of sabotage carried out by extremist groups setting fire to vehicles and homes undermine regional stability, endanger lives and seriously harm Israel's national security and foreign relations," he wrote on X.
Eisenkot was tasked with forming Israel's next government on 8 November by President Isaac Herzog.
He accused National Security Minister Ben Gvir and Finance Minister Smotrich of bringing the West Bank "to the brink of unchecked anarchy".
"This reality is not inevitable," he said, describing it as the consequence of poor leadership.
He said authorities should use all available measures, including administrative detention and targeted operations by the Shin Bet, Israel’s domestic security agency, to stop the perpetrators.

Pro-Israel Hakeem Jeffries says he will push legislation targeting settler violence
Pro-Israel US Democratic leader, Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to become the first Black speaker of the House of Representatives next year, has pledged to advance legislation targeting Israeli settler violence in the occupied West Bank within the first 100 days of the new Congress.
In an interview with The New York Times, Jeffries said the West Bank Settler Violence Protection and Prevention Act should be among the early legislative priorities, adding that he expected strong support for it within the House Democratic Caucus.
Jeffries also described the devastation inflicted on Palestinian civilians in Gaza as “unacceptable, unsustainable and un-American”, calling for increased humanitarian assistance, medical aid, housing support and access to clean water and air.
Asked whether he supported the proposed Block the Bombs and Stop the Settlements bills, which call for restricting arms sale to Israel and broader sanctions on settlement expansion, Jeffries said he had not taken a position.
On calls to halt US weapons exports used in regional conflicts, he said the current approach was “not sustainable” and needed to change.
More than a million people have signed a petition urging Democrats to reject Hakeem Jeffries as the next Speaker of the US House of Representative. An Economist/YouGov poll published last month found that Jeffries had just a 26 percent approval rating among registered voters.
Critics say that one reason Jeffries' popularity has taken a hit is that he is an avid supporter of Israel.
The American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac) ranks among his top campaign-financing contributors.
Jeffries said he expects strong support for the West Bank Settler Violence Protection and Prevention Act. (AFP)

Lebanese President Joseph Aoun has accused Iran of meddling in Lebanon's affairs through Hezbollah's weapons and also demanded Israel withdraw from the country's south.
In a speech on the eve of Lebanon's 83rd independence anniversary, Aoun vowed to press ahead with plans to bring all weapons under state control.
Lebanon's sovereignty still faces two threats, he said: "The Israeli occupation of parts of our territory" and foreign interference from "influential elements within the Iranian regime" through weapons and decisions outside the authority of the Lebanese state.
On Israel, Aoun stressed Lebanon's message was clear and direct: "Withdraw from every inch of Lebanese territory. Stop your attacks."
There would be "no occupation ever again", he said. "And no weapons outside the state that... serve the interests of, foreign powers," he added, without naming a specific group.
Such weapons may once have served a purpose, he said, but later imposed a high cost on Lebanon when they came to serve causes beyond its borders.
"You must hand over your weapons," Aoun said.
The Lebanese government has committed to disarming Hezbollah, whose arsenal has long outstripped that of the national army and which has justified its weapons as necessary to resist Israel.
In June, Lebanon and Israel signed a framework agreement that included the disarmament of Hezbollah, a gradual Israeli withdrawal from territories it occupies in the south and the deployment of the Lebanese army to the area.
But implementation has stalled and Hezbollah has refused to surrender its weapons.
Israel's army still carries out strikes, shelling and detonations in the south, where its forces are operating in a self-declared "security zone" running around 10 kilometres.
Report by AFP

UK, France and China vote against UAE's Lana Nusseibeh at UN

Along with the US and Russia, the countries make up three of the P5, the permanent members of the UN Security Council that can veto any prospective candidate for the world body's top job.
While votes in the straw poll are cast anonymously, diplomatic and other sources close to the Security Council told Middle East Eye that the UK, China and France were the P5 members who had voted to "discourage" Nusseibeh's candidacy.
The US, Russia and Israel - which is not currently part of the Security Council and thus does not vote - all back Nusseibeh, according to the same sources.
In total, the UAE minister of state and former ambassador to the UN received seven "encourage" votes, six "discourage" votes and two "no opinion" votes - the same result she achieved in the last straw poll, held on 6 November.

White phosphorus can cause severe burns, ignite repeatedly and produce intense heat and toxic smoke.
Human rights groups and The New York Times said in June they have documented Israel's use of the chemical white phosphorus over civilian areas in Lebanon.
White phosphorus is not banned under international law, but it is illegal to use the chemical in and near populated areas since it can cause widespread harm. Israel has been accused by the international human rights community for decades of using the substance in a way that puts civilians in danger.
In a working paper submitted at the review session for the UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, the group said the current treaty has glaring gaps that allow for the use of white phosphorus.

Gaza Board of Peace says it will hand keys to UN if Israel fails to honour commitments
A senior adviser to the Trump-appointed Gaza Peace Council has warned that the body could return responsibility for the enclave to the United Nations if Israel does not honour its commitments under the 20-point plan, Israeli outlet Ynet has reported.
Josh Gruenbaum, who was appointed to the council by Trump and previously worked in the White House, told Ynet: “We have been extremely patient and have given Israel its space. But it is frustrating that now with the elections behind us — even if they haven’t resulted in a clear coalition — that Israel is failing to move forward on the commitments Netanyahu made to President Trump.”
“If this political leadership says it no longer wants to honour what they committed to, just let us know,” Gruenbaum said “And we will throw the keys back to the UN.”
Ynet said it had seen a presentation prepared by council members, who visited Israel last week. Its final slide, titled “Other alternatives to Gaza”, reportedly lists several scenarios if the plan is abandoned.
These include a future US administration and Congress ordering a different reconstruction plan, the UN Security Council taking over “perhaps through UNRWA”, the Palestinian Authority and Hamas.
The last scenario, according to the slide, is that Israel becomes fully responsible for the administrative and humanitarian costs of Gaza’s population.
Another slide reportedly says Hamas formally accepted the plan in July, pledging to give up its weapons and transfer governmental powers to the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG), the technocratic body meant to run the territory.
“We are at a standstill due to political elements within the Netanyahu government who have prevented us from progressing and from testing whether Hamas will keep its word,” Gruenbaum said, according to Ynet.
Gruenbaum also criticises Israel for failing to allow sufficient aid into Gaza before winter

Israel has not acted on calls to protect Palestinian olive farmers, Ocha says
Calls on the Israeli authorities to protect Palestinian olive farmers and ensure they can reach their groves safely have not been acted upon, the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (Ocha) said, citing the Humanitarian Country Team.
Instead, in the first nine months of 2026, Israeli authorities uprooted or otherwise damaged more than 10,000 Palestinian-owned trees and saplings across the West Bank, mostly olives, the statement adds.
The Humanitarian Country Team for the Occupied Palestinian Territory, which brings together UN bodies and humanitarian NGOs, said more than 400 Israeli settler attacks on the Palestinian olive harvest since September have resulted in casualties or damage to property, including to more than 4,000 trees and saplings.
The number of attacks this year exceeds that recorded in any previous olive harvest season. This year’s harvesting window is closing, the team said, but there is still some time to act.
"Humanitarian NGOs and UN agencies urge the Israeli authorities in the strongest possible terms: end all attacks on Palestinians and their livelihoods, as required by international law. Ensure farmers have free, safe, sufficient and reliable access to their land. The team added that perpetrators must be stopped and held to account," the statement read.

In its weekly report published on Friday, UKMTO said four of the six incidents occurred in the Strait of Hormuz and two in the Arabian Gulf.
The UKMTO recorded 115 outbound and 148 inbound transits during the seven days to November 18, including US-facilitated movements. The combined figure was down from 139 outbound and 169 inbound the previous week.

Vance refuses to endorse Iran strikes despite pressure from Trump
US Vice President JD Vance on Friday declined to say whether he would have authorised strikes on Iran to stop it developing a nuclear weapon, sidestepping Trump’s calls for him to say the attacks were necessary and that he would carry them out again.
Speaking at a White House press conference alongside Trump, Vance said the decision to attack Iran in February had been the president’s call, “and my job is to support the president of the United States”.
After the midterm elections, Vance blamed the war for the Republicans’ historic losses and called for the US to exit the conflict.
His statement, posted on social media, was widely seen as a break with Trump as the vice president weighs a 2028 White House bid.
“The reason we lost is the war,” Vance wrote. “The president himself said so last night. If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next six years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay.”
Trump said on Friday that he was not unhappy with Vance’s conclusion but that it lacked a crucial element: an acknowledgement that the strikes were necessary and that Vance would make the same decision.
“People that work for me, they have a right to their opinion,” Trump said. “But I say, I know the Iranians, and, frankly, they’re crazy.”
Vice President JD Vance on Iran: "The goal of keeping Iran from getting a nuclear weapon is absolutely what we need to be doing. It's the biggest state sponsored terrorism. If they had a nuclear weapon, they would use it as leverage or God forbid they would attack and kill thousands, hundreds of thousands potentially, of innocent people. The president is the one who makes the decision and the president has said he would do it again. And my view is that my goal is and my job is to support the President of the United States."
— Vice President JD Vance (@VP) November 20, 2026

Iran wants Trump to state explicitly he wants a deal, Araghchi says
Iran still has hope that diplomacy can end its war with the United States, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said, adding that the two sides are still exchanging messages through mediators.
“We are seeking an agreement with the US that would ensure there is no further war afterwards,” Araghchi told an Iranian newspaper.
He said Tehran saw no need to change the intermediaries in the talks.
Before going any further, Iran wants guarantees that Washington is serious about negotiating, he said, and it has discussed the form and nature of possible confidence-building measures with the mediators.
Iran’s first demand is for US President Donald Trump to state explicitly that he wants an agreement, Araghchi said.
He added that it was not surprising for Trump to take a new position every day, or even to reverse what he had said the day before.
One of Iran’s red lines is that its enriched uranium must not leave the country, Araghchi stated, though he believed a fair solution could be reached.
He also said the Strait of Hormuz would remain closed until the US met Iran’s seven conditions.
His comments came hours after Trump reiterated that the US had "total control" over the strait.
Iran’s official position on the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons remains the same, and its nuclear doctrine has not changed, Araghchi added.

If US President Donald Trump has his way, Baran* will be out of business.
The thirty-year-old Kurd is a trader who buys diesel in Iraq and sells it in Afghanistan. It’s a stressful gig, but one that can generate a tidy profit in a place like Iraqi Kurdistan. A truck laden with $20,000 worth of diesel in Iraq can sell in Kabul for around $24,000, leaving around $2,000 for the trader once expenses are paid. But it has to make it through Iran first.
“The journey is more dangerous now. It’s harder to find drivers. The border isn’t as reliable. The price of diesel has also shot up,” Baran, whose name has been changed to protect his identity, told Middle East Eye.
Trump says instead of restarting strikes on Iran, he wants to choke its economy. In addition to a naval blockade, the US is pressing countries like Turkey, Iraq and Pakistan to seal their borders with Iran. Earlier this month, the US announced a task force to blockade trade across Iran’s land borders and the Caspian Sea.
Baran has no political beef with the US. On the contrary, he says, “George W. Bush overthrew Saddam Hussein. He helped Kurdistan. I don’t prefer Iran to the US,” he said over a glass of anise-flavoured Arak and hookahs at a restaurant in Sulaymaniyah.
“But this war has not been good for business or our economy.”
Baran is a microcosm of the city he calls home.

Palestinian man killed near Ramallah as Israeli raids sweep occupied West Bank
A Palestinian man was killed by Israeli forces near Ramallah on Friday as the forces carried out raids, detentions and a home demolition across the occupied West Bank, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.
Hamza Masoud Salim Abdo, 42, was killed in Dura al-Qare, northeast of Ramallah, by Israeli forces who are still withholding his body, the Palestinian General Authority of Civil Affairs said.
In Jaba, south of Jenin, Israeli forces beat a man who was taken to hospital, the Palestinian Red Crescent said. A convoy of army vehicles later stormed the town and detained two young men. In nearby Qabatiya, soldiers fired on a vehicle and detained two people.
In Jericho, a young Palestinian man was shot in the foot during a raid on the al-Bayader neighbourhood.
South of Hebron, Israeli forces raided al-Fawwar refugee camp as residents left Friday prayers, firing tear gas and beating a young man who was later hospitalised.
In nearby Beit Ummar, Israeli forces stormed the town, ordered merchants to close their shops and fired barrages of tear gas and stun grenades, according to local media activist Mohammad Awad. He said soldiers severely beat and detained two men, aged 22 and 45.
In the Tulkarm governorate, several young men were detained as Israeli forces raided the town of Anabta.
Also on Friday, Israeli bulldozers demolished a home in al-Mazra’a al-Gharbiya, northwest of Ramallah.
Meanwhile, Israeli settlers stole the contents of a roadside fruit stand south of Jenin and trees from a nursery in Jaba, surveillance footage showed.

A new study by Pew Research Center has become a trigger for Islamophobic attacks from many online after it projected that Muslims will outnumber Christians by 2035.
The study on the future of world religions between 2020 and 2070 projects that Muslims will grow to 3.6 billion worldwide by 2070, growing by 80 percent, prompted by their dual demographic of youth and high fertility.
The study also showcases that Pakistan will surpass Indonesia as the country with the most Muslims by 2070.
In North America, Muslims will more than triple in number, with migration playing a big role, growing by nine million in the US, but will still make up only four percent of the country’s total population. Currently, Muslims only make up 1-1.6 percent of the total US population.
Right-wing commentators and politicians immediately took to social media to express their “concern” over the study’s projections, despite the report stating that Muslims would make up only a small percentage of the US population.
